strengths: The paper addresses an important question: how adversarial training can preserve clean generalization while exhibiting a large robust generalization gap. The explicit CGRO definition makes the target phenomenon clear.

Combining representation complexity with training dynamics is conceptually useful. Partial signal learning followed by instance-specific noise memorization offers an interpretable mechanism worth investigating.
The MNIST/CIFAR10 capacity experiments, synthetic feature trajectories, and supplementary loss-landscape measurements provide complementary illustrations of the phenomenon.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.4 is false under the stated assumptions. Consider a distribution on two well-separated atoms, one per class, and a clean linear separator whose boundary lies within δ of one atom. This satisfies Assumptions 4.1–4.3. With a growing sample, both atoms have empirical frequencies near one half, so vanishing robust training error forces zero robust test error; no CGRO classifier exists. The construction needs an additional assumption ensuring sufficient population mass remains vulnerable after training neighborhoods are memorized.

The representation proof has further substantive gaps. Appendix F claims uniform o(1) approximation of the generally discontinuous indicator-based classifier by continuous ReLU networks, which cannot hold across nonvanishing jumps. Also, Assumption 4.2 separates opposite classes only; it does not imply that all training balls are disjoint, as Lemma 4.5 claims. Same-class overlaps invalidate the subsequent algebraic rewriting. A corrected construction and classification-margin argument are needed.

Theorem 5.9 does not establish the robust training guarantee in Definition 3.3. Training attacks are restricted to the signal direction and leave memorized noise unchanged, whereas the claimed guarantee concerns the full perturbation ball. Indeed, under the asserted scalings, the total noise norm is o(α) and δ approaches α. A full ℓ2 attack can reverse the noise and simultaneously reduce the signal to o(α), making the margin negative when U=Θ(α^-q) and V_i=Θ(1). Thus the claimed learned features contradict low full-ball robust training error.

The clean-generalization proof in Theorem E.12 uses an invalid concentration argument: a cubic polynomial of Gaussian noise is not generally sub-Gaussian. Projections across filters also share the same noise and cannot be treated as independent contributions. Additionally, V_i=Θ(1) does not establish the claimed Θ(1) norm for every filter's orthogonal component. These steps directly support the central o(1) clean test error conclusion.

The synthetic experiment sets δ=α=10, violating the theorem's requirement δ<α and allowing complete removal of the meaningful signal patch. It therefore does not validate the claimed regime. The real-data capacity and flatness curves are suggestive but do not establish the proposed mechanism. Missing PGD step counts, step sizes, restarts, seed variability, and synthetic test-set size also limit reproducibility and confidence in the robustness estimates.

The originality and interpretation of the exponential lower bound need clarification. Theorem 4.7 is an existential worst-case result closely following Li et al. (2022); replacing linear separability with an assumption that includes it does not itself strengthen that statement. The paper also does not connect this hard distribution to the structured distribution used for its dynamics analysis. Consequently, the combined complexity hierarchy does not establish the proposed explanation for typical adversarial training.
